tips.title: Energy flows, materials cycle
tips.body: Energy arrives from the Sun continuously and is **lost** as heat; materials are **already here** and must be **reused**. That one contrast answers *why must materials cycle* and frames every cycle in the topic.

tips.title: Only photosynthesis takes carbon out
tips.body: Respiration, combustion and decomposition all **return** carbon dioxide; **photosynthesis** is the only process that removes it. If your carbon cycle has two arrows going into the plants, one of them is wrong.

tips.title: Decomposers close the carbon and nitrogen cycles
tips.body: Asked why microorganisms matter, the answer is the same each time: **without them the elements stay locked inside dead organisms**. A carbon or nitrogen cycle described without decomposers has no way of getting the elements back.

tips.title: Plants take nitrogen up as nitrates
tips.body: The air is 78% nitrogen and plants cannot use any of it, because **N₂ is unreactive**. Most of the nitrogen cycle is about turning nitrogen into **nitrates** in the soil — which is what the question is really asking.

tips.title: Grams per day is not percent per day
tips.body: A decay question that gives a **starting mass** is often asking for a **percentage** rate. Work out which unit is wanted before dividing: $60$ g over $6$ days is **10 g/day**, but also **5% per day** of a 200 g sample.

why.matters:
The Earth gains energy from the Sun continuously and gains almost no **matter** at all. Every carbon atom in you was in something else before, and will be in something else afterwards — so the same atoms have to be used again and again.

That is what a material cycle is, and it is why decomposers matter as much as producers. A world with photosynthesis and no decay would lock every nutrient into dead bodies within a few generations and stop.

examples.title: Why a compost heap gets hot
examples.body:
A heap of grass cuttings warms up in the middle, sometimes enough to steam. Nothing has caught fire: **microorganisms** are respiring, and respiration releases energy.

That is decay seen from the inside. Decomposers break down the dead material and return its carbon to the air as carbon dioxide and its nitrogen to the soil as compounds plants can use. The heat is the by-product — and it is also why a heap rots faster when it is turned, since the microorganisms need oxygen and warmth as much as anything else does.

visual.alt: A flow chart of decay in a compost heap: microorganisms respire the dead plant material, giving off carbon dioxide and the heat that warms the heap, and returning nutrients to the soil

examples.title: Why a farmer puts nitrogen back
examples.body:
In a wood, the nitrogen a plant takes up returns to the soil when the plant dies. In a field, the crop is **harvested and taken away**, and the nitrogen in it goes with it.

So the cycle is broken on purpose, and something has to close it: fertiliser, manure, or a crop of clover or beans whose root nodules hold **nitrogen-fixing bacteria**. That is why crop rotation exists and why a fertiliser bag has a number for nitrogen on it. Farming is a material cycle with a hole in it, deliberately patched.

visual.alt: A table contrasting a wood, where a plant decays where it stood and its nitrogen returns to the same soil, with a field, where the crop is harvested and removed so the nitrogen has to be put back

examples.title: Why water is a cycle you can watch
examples.body:
The water cycle is the one that needs no microorganisms and happens where you can see it: evaporation from the sea and from leaves, condensation into cloud, precipitation, and the run-off back to the sea.

It matters here because it is the same idea stripped of biology — the same molecules going round, driven by energy from the Sun, with no source and no sink. And it is the cycle that moves the others: nitrogen and carbon compounds are carried in water, which is why drainage decides so much about a soil.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the water cycle: evaporation from the sea, condensation into cloud, precipitation on to the land and run-off back to the sea, driven by energy from the Sun

steps.title: Why materials must cycle
steps.body:
An ecosystem receives a constant supply of **energy** from the Sun, but it receives no new supply of **materials**. The carbon, water and nitrogen on Earth now are the same atoms that have always been here.

So every element a living thing is built from must be **used, released and used again**. Materials **cycle** through the **biotic** components — the living organisms — and the **abiotic** components — the air, water, rocks and soil.

That contrast is the heart of this topic and worth stating plainly:

**Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost. Materials cycle round and are reused.**

**Decomposers** are what makes the cycling possible. When an organism dies, the elements in it are locked inside its tissues. **Microorganisms** — bacteria and fungi — break the dead material down, releasing the elements back into the soil and the air where plants can take them up again.

Without decomposers, every element would end up locked in dead bodies and the cycles would stop. That is why microorganisms appear in both the carbon and the nitrogen cycles.

steps.title: The carbon cycle
steps.body:
Four processes move carbon, and only **one** of them takes carbon dioxide **out** of the air. Knowing which way each goes is most of the marks.

**Removing carbon dioxide from the air:**

- **Photosynthesis.** Plants and algae take in CO₂ and use the carbon to make glucose, and from that all their other compounds. Carbon is now in the **biotic** part of the ecosystem.

**Returning carbon dioxide to the air:**

- **Respiration.** Every living organism — plants, animals and microorganisms — releases CO₂.
- **Combustion.** Burning wood or fossil fuels releases the carbon locked in them.
- **Decomposition.** Microorganisms break down dead organisms and waste, respiring as they do, which releases CO₂.

Carbon moves along a food chain when an animal **eats** a plant or another animal.

**Fossil fuels** are the slow branch of the cycle: organisms that died and were buried before they could decompose, their carbon locked away for millions of years. **Combustion** returns it all at once — which is why burning them raises atmospheric CO₂ faster than photosynthesis can remove it.

**The role of decomposers**, which the spec names specifically: without them, carbon would remain locked in dead organisms and would not return to the air or the soil at all.

steps.title: The water cycle, and getting drinking water
steps.body:
The water cycle has four processes, and the specification adds a practical question on the end of it.

- **Evaporation.** The Sun's energy turns liquid water from seas, lakes and rivers into water vapour.
- **Transpiration.** Water evaporates from the leaves of plants, adding to the vapour in the air.
- **Condensation.** As the vapour rises it cools, and turns back into tiny droplets, forming clouds.
- **Precipitation.** The droplets join, become heavy, and fall as rain, snow or hail.

The water then flows back to the sea through rivers and through the ground, and the cycle repeats.

**Why it matters.** The water cycle carries **fresh water from the sea onto the land**. That supplies the water plants need for photosynthesis and for support, and the water animals need to drink, and it refills rivers, lakes and groundwater. Evaporation leaves the salt behind, so the rain that falls is fresh.

**Potable water.** *Potable* means **safe to drink** — which is not the same as **pure**. Potable water contains dissolved substances; it simply has low enough levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms to be safe.

**In areas of drought**, where there is not enough fresh water, drinking water can be produced from **sea water** by **desalination** — removing the salt. Two methods:

- **Distillation**: the sea water is heated until it evaporates, and the vapour is condensed, leaving the salt behind.
- **Reverse osmosis**: the water is forced at high pressure through a membrane that lets water through but not the dissolved salts.

Both work, and both have the same drawback: they need **a great deal of energy**, which makes them **expensive**. That is why desalination is used where there is no alternative rather than everywhere.

steps.title: The nitrogen cycle
steps.body:
Plants need **nitrogen** to make proteins, and the air is **78% nitrogen** — but they cannot use it. Nitrogen gas, N₂, is **unreactive**, so plants can only take nitrogen up from the soil as **nitrates**.

The question the spec asks is therefore: **how are nitrates made available for plant uptake?** There are four answers, and three of them involve bacteria.

**1. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria.** They convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds. Some live **free in the soil**; others live in **root nodules of legumes** — peas, beans, clover — in the mutualistic relationship from the last topic.

**2. Decomposers.** Bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste, releasing the nitrogen in their proteins as **ammonia**.

**3. Nitrifying bacteria.** They convert that **ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates**, which is the form plants can absorb.

**4. Fertilisers.** Farmers add nitrates directly to the soil. This works quickly, but excess can be washed into rivers, causing algae to grow and then decompose, using up the oxygen.

There is also a process going the other way: **denitrifying bacteria** in waterlogged soils convert nitrates back into **nitrogen gas**, which is why good drainage matters to a farmer.

**Crop rotation** is the farming practice the spec names. Growing a **legume** in a field every few years lets its root-nodule bacteria fix nitrogen, restoring the soil's nitrates naturally rather than by adding fertiliser. Growing the same crop every year drains the soil of the nutrients that crop uses.

steps.title: Decay, and its rate
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* This section covers spec points 9.17B to 9.19B.

Decomposition is carried out by **microorganisms**, so anything that affects how well microorganisms live and work affects the **rate of decay**. Three factors are named:

- **Temperature.** Warmer is faster, because the microorganisms' enzymes work faster — but only **up to a point**. Too hot and those enzymes **denature**, so decay slows or stops.
- **Water content.** Moist is faster: microorganisms need water to live, and they secrete enzymes into their surroundings which need water to work.
- **Oxygen availability.** More oxygen is faster, because most decomposers respire **aerobically**.

The same three facts explain **both** applications the spec names, in opposite directions.

**Food preservation** slows decay down: a **fridge or freezer** lowers the temperature; **drying** removes the water; **canning** heats the food to kill the microorganisms and seals it from the air; **vacuum packing** removes the oxygen.

**Composting** speeds decay up: a compost heap is kept **moist**, **turned** to let air in, and built large enough to stay **warm**.

steps.title: Going deeper: the shape behind all three cycles
steps.body:
**Every cycle has the same two halves.** Once you see it, three cycles become one idea:

- Something **takes the element out of the abiotic world and into living things**.
- Something **returns it**.


And **decomposers appear in both the carbon and nitrogen cycles**, because they are what unlocks the elements held in dead organisms. If a question asks why microorganisms matter in a cycle, that is the answer: **without them the elements stay locked in dead material.**

**Why the carbon cycle is out of balance.** Photosynthesis and respiration roughly balanced each other for a very long time. Two human activities have upset it:

- **Burning fossil fuels** releases carbon that had been locked away for millions of years, far faster than photosynthesis removes it.
- **Deforestation** removes the trees that would have taken CO₂ back out, and burning them releases more.

So the imbalance is not that respiration has increased, but that a **slow branch of the cycle has been short-circuited**. That framing is what a top answer offers instead of *humans produce carbon dioxide*.

**Why fertiliser is not simply good.** Adding nitrates raises crop yields, but excess is washed into rivers. There, it makes **algae grow rapidly**, blocking light from the plants below; those plants die, **decomposers multiply** to break them down, and the decomposers' **respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen** — so fish and other animals suffocate. The chain of reasoning, not the word, is what carries the marks.

**Decay: warmer is faster, until it is not.** This is the one graph shape worth holding: the rate of decay rises with temperature, reaches a **peak**, and then falls **sharply** as the microorganisms' enzymes **denature**. It is the same shape as an enzyme rate graph — because it *is* one.

**Read the rate question.** *Grams per day* and *percent per day* are different quantities, and a question that gives a starting mass is often asking for the second. Check the unit you have been asked for before dividing.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Energy flows** through an ecosystem and is lost; **materials cycle** and are reused, because there is no new supply.
- **Decomposers** unlock the elements held in dead organisms, which is why they appear in both the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
- **Carbon cycle**: only **photosynthesis** removes CO₂. **Respiration**, **combustion** and **decomposition** return it.
- **Fossil fuels** hold carbon locked away for millions of years; **combustion** returns it far faster than photosynthesis can remove it.
- **Water cycle**: **evaporation**, **transpiration**, **condensation**, **precipitation**.
- **Potable** means **safe to drink**, not pure.
- In drought, **desalination** by **distillation** or **reverse osmosis** makes sea water drinkable — both need a great deal of **energy**.
- Plants cannot use nitrogen gas; they take nitrogen up as **nitrates**.
- **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** make nitrogen compounds from the air, free in soil or in **root nodules of legumes**.
- **Decomposers** release **ammonia**; **nitrifying bacteria** turn it into **nitrates**; **denitrifying bacteria** turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas.
- **Fertilisers** add nitrates quickly, but excess washes into rivers and causes oxygen to be used up.
- **Crop rotation** with a **legume** restores nitrates naturally.
- **Biology only — decay** is faster when **warm** (until enzymes denature), **moist**, and with **oxygen**.
- **Food preservation** works against the three factors (a fridge, drying, vacuum packing; canning heats and seals); **composting** provides all three.
- $\text{rate of decay} = \dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{time}}$.

questions.prompt: Describe the carbon cycle, naming the processes that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and those that return it, and explain the role of microorganisms.
questions.solution: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis, which is carried out by plants and algae. They use the carbon from the carbon dioxide to make glucose and from that all the other carbon compounds in their bodies, so the carbon becomes part of the living, or biotic, part of the ecosystem. Carbon then passes along food chains when animals eat plants or other animals. Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere by three processes. The first is respiration, which is carried out by all living organisms, including plants, animals and microorganisms. The second is combustion, the burning of wood or of fossil fuels, which releases the carbon that had been locked up in them. The third is decomposition. Microorganisms, which are bacteria and fungi acting as decomposers, break down dead organisms and their waste, and as they respire they release carbon dioxide back into the air. Microorganisms are essential to the cycle because without them the carbon in dead organisms would stay locked inside their bodies and would never be returned to the atmosphere or the soil for plants to use again.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Removing carbon dioxide.** Only **photosynthesis**, carried out by **plants and algae**. The carbon becomes glucose and then every other carbon compound in the plant — so it is now in the **biotic** part of the ecosystem.

**Moving along the chain.** Carbon passes on when an animal **eats** a plant or another animal.

**Returning carbon dioxide.** Three processes:

- **Respiration**, by **all** living organisms — plants and microorganisms included, not just animals.
- **Combustion**, burning wood or fossil fuels, releasing the carbon locked in them.
- **Decomposition**, as microorganisms break down dead material and respire.

**The role of microorganisms.** Bacteria and fungi acting as **decomposers** unlock the carbon held in dead organisms. Without them it would **stay locked inside dead bodies** and never return to the air or soil for plants to use again.

That last point is what the spec means by *the role of microorganisms as decomposers*, and it is a mark in its own right — a description of the cycle that never says why they matter has left it behind.

questions.prompt: Explain how temperature, water content and oxygen availability affect the rate of decay, and explain how these three factors are used both to preserve food and to make compost.
questions.solution: Decay is carried out by microorganisms, so anything that affects how well they live and work affects the rate of decay. A higher temperature increases the rate because the enzymes of the microorganisms work faster, but only up to a point, because above a certain temperature those enzymes denature and the rate falls sharply. A higher water content increases the rate because microorganisms need water to survive, and because the enzymes they release into the material around them need water in order to work. A greater availability of oxygen increases the rate because most decomposers respire aerobically and so need oxygen to release the energy they require. Food preservation works by reversing all three of these. A fridge or freezer lowers the temperature so the enzymes work more slowly. Drying or salting removes the water the microorganisms need. Vacuum packing removes the oxygen so that aerobic decomposers cannot respire, and canning heats the food to kill the microorganisms and then seals it from the air. Composting works by providing all three instead. The heap is kept moist, it is turned regularly so that air and therefore oxygen can get in, and it is built large enough that the heat released by the microorganisms keeps it warm.

**Why these three.** Decay is done by **microorganisms**, so whatever affects how well they live and work sets the rate.

- **Temperature.** Warmer is faster, because their **enzymes** work faster — but only **up to a point**. Above it the enzymes **denature** and the rate falls sharply.
- **Water content.** Moist is faster: microorganisms need water to live, and the enzymes they release into the material need water to work.
- **Oxygen.** More is faster, because most decomposers respire **aerobically**.

**Food preservation works against all three.**

- A **fridge or freezer** lowers the temperature, slowing the enzymes.
- **Drying or salting** removes the water.
- **Vacuum packing** removes the oxygen; **canning** heats the food to kill the microorganisms, then seals it from the air.

**Composting provides all three.**

- The heap is kept **moist**.
- It is **turned** so air, and therefore oxygen, gets in.
- It is built **large** enough that the heat the microorganisms release keeps it **warm**.

Notice that the two applications are the same three facts used in opposite directions — which is why they are worth learning once rather than twice.

questions.prompt:
A student measured the mass of a bag of leaves as it decayed.

| Day | Mass (g) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 250 |
| 4 | 214 |
| 8 | 178 |
| 12 | 160 |

Calculate the mean rate of decay over the first 8 days, as a percentage of the starting mass lost per day.
questions.solution: Mass lost in 8 days $= 250 - 178 = 72$ g. As a percentage of the starting mass: $\dfrac{72}{250} \times 100 = 28.8\%$ over 8 days. Per day: $28.8 \div 8 = 3.6\%$ per day. (The table also shows decay slowing later: only 18 g is lost between day 8 and day 12.)

markScheme.description: finds the mass lost, 72 g
divides by the starting mass and by 8 days

questions.prompt: What do denitrifying bacteria do?
questions.solution: **Denitrifying** bacteria turn nitrates back into **nitrogen gas**. They thrive in waterlogged soil with little oxygen, which is why good drainage keeps nitrates in the soil for crops.

markScheme.description: nitrates into nitrogen gas

options: Turn nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds
Turn ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates
Break down dead material, releasing ammonia
Turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas

questions.prompt: Why is desalination used only where there is no other source of fresh water?
questions.solution: Both distillation and reverse osmosis need **a great deal of energy**, so they are **expensive**. They do make sea water safe to drink, which is why they are used in drought.

markScheme.description: it needs a lot of energy, so it is expensive

options: It leaves too much salt in the water to drink
It needs a lot of energy, so it is expensive
It only works on water from rivers and lakes
It removes the minerals that make water safe

questions.prompt: Why does the water cycle matter to living things on land?
questions.solution: Evaporation leaves the salt behind, so the water cycle carries **fresh water from the sea onto the land** as rain, supplying plants and animals and refilling rivers, lakes and groundwater.

markScheme.description: it carries fresh water from the sea onto the land

options: It removes carbon dioxide from the air over the sea
It turns nitrogen gas into nitrates
It carries fresh water from the sea to land
It adds salt to rivers and lakes

questions.prompt: How does salting food slow down its decay?
questions.solution: Salt draws **water** out of the food and out of the microorganisms by osmosis. Microorganisms need water to live and for their enzymes to work, so decay slows. It is the same factor that **drying** removes.

markScheme.description: removes water, which microorganisms need

options: It draws water out, so microorganisms cannot grow
It removes the oxygen from inside the food
It lowers the temperature of the food to fridge level
It adds nitrates that poison the bacteria

questions.prompt: A farmer's field stays waterlogged for several weeks. Afterwards the crop shows signs of a shortage of nitrogen. Which explanation fits best?
questions.solution: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, which suits **denitrifying bacteria**. They turn **nitrates** back into **nitrogen gas**, which the crop cannot use, so the soil loses the nitrates the plants need. Good drainage prevents it.

markScheme.description: denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates into nitrogen gas

options: Nitrifying bacteria made far too many nitrates
Denitrifying bacteria turned nitrates into nitrogen gas
The water dissolved the nitrogen gas so roots absorbed it
Legume root nodules released too much ammonia

questions.prompt: Which process returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere from living plants, animals and microorganisms?
questions.solution: **Respiration.** Every living organism respires, breaking down glucose to release energy, and carbon dioxide is a product of aerobic respiration. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise; animals respire the carbon compounds they ate; and the decomposer microorganisms respire as they break down dead material and waste, which is how the carbon in dead organisms gets back into the air. Photosynthesis does the opposite, taking carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. Evaporation is part of the water cycle, and nitrogen fixation is part of the nitrogen cycle; neither moves carbon.

markScheme.description: respiration

options: Photosynthesis
Evaporation
Nitrogen fixation
Respiration

questions.prompt: Most of the water that falls as rain on land evaporated from the salty sea, yet rain is fresh water with almost no dissolved salt. Why?
questions.solution: **Only the water evaporates; the dissolved salts stay behind in the sea.** Evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour, which rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation. The salt does not evaporate, so the sea stays salty and the rain is fresh. This is the same principle that desalination by distillation uses to make potable water in areas of drought: sea water is heated, the water vapour is collected and condensed, and the salt is left behind. Clouds do not filter anything, plants do not take salt out of rain, and the sea is salty at every depth.

markScheme.description: only the water evaporates, and the dissolved salts are left behind in the sea

options: The salt evaporates too, but it is filtered out as the water vapour passes through clouds
Only the water evaporates, and the dissolved salts are left behind in the sea
Rain is salty when it falls, and plants remove the salt as the water soaks into the soil
The sea is only salty near the surface, and the water evaporates from deep below it

questions.prompt: Slices of cooked ham keep for much longer in a sealed vacuum pack than on an open plate in the same fridge. Why does the vacuum pack slow the decay?
questions.solution: **Removing the air removes the oxygen.** Decay is caused by microorganisms, bacteria and fungi, growing on the food and digesting it. Most of them respire **aerobically**, so they need oxygen to release the energy they use to grow and multiply. In a vacuum pack there is almost no oxygen, so they grow very slowly and the ham lasts longer; the fridge adds a second brake by keeping the temperature low. A vacuum does not dry the ham, which stays moist inside the pack; the plastic releases nothing that kills bacteria; and a sealed pack is at the same temperature as the rest of the fridge. Temperature, water content and oxygen availability are the three factors that control the rate of decomposition, and this method works on the third.

markScheme.description: removing the air removes oxygen, so the decomposer microorganisms cannot respire aerobically and multiply quickly

options: Removing the air removes oxygen, so the microorganisms that decompose the ham cannot respire aerobically and multiply quickly
The vacuum pulls the water out of the ham, so the microorganisms that decompose it have no water in which to grow
The plastic of the pack slowly releases a chemical that kills any bacteria and fungi landing on the ham
A sealed pack keeps the ham several degrees colder than the open air inside the rest of the fridge

questions.prompt: A gardener notices that the middle of a large heap of grass cuttings is hot to the touch, even on a cold day, and that the heap cools down after a few weeks. Which statement explains the heat?
questions.skill: where the heat in a compost heap comes from
questions.solution: **The decomposer microorganisms respire, and respiration releases heat.** Bacteria and fungi in the heap digest the cuttings and respire the sugars they absorb, releasing energy, and some of that energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat. In a large heap the heat cannot escape quickly, so the middle warms up, and the warmth in turn speeds up the microorganisms' enzymes, so decay gets faster still, until the heap is so hot that the enzymes begin to denature. After a few weeks the easily digested material has been used up, so respiration slows and the heap cools. Plants do not store the sun's heat in their tissues, water does not react with cellulose to give out heat, and the soil beneath a heap is not warm in winter.

markScheme.description: the decomposer microorganisms respire as they break the cuttings down, and respiration releases energy, some of it as heat

options: The grass absorbed heat from the sun while it was growing and releases that stored heat slowly as it breaks down
Water in the heap reacts chemically with the cellulose in the plant cell walls, and the reaction gives out heat
Microorganisms respire as they break the cuttings down, and respiration releases energy, some of it as heat
The heap is warmed from below by the soil, which stays warm throughout the year however cold the air is

questions.prompt: Name the swellings on the roots of peas, beans and clover that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
questions.solution: **Root nodules.** Peas, beans and clover are legumes. The nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in the nodules on their roots convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds that the plant can use to make amino acids and proteins; in return the bacteria receive sugars from the plant, so the relationship is a mutualism. This is why growing a legume as part of a crop rotation, and ploughing it back in, raises the amount of nitrate in the soil for the following crop.

markScheme.description: root nodules

questions.prompt: An apple with a mass of 250 g is left in a warm room. After four weeks it has decayed and its mass is 190 g. Calculate the percentage of the apple's original mass that has been lost.
questions.skill: percentage loss of mass in decay
questions.solution: Mass lost $= 250 - 190 = 60$ g. Percentage lost $= \dfrac{60}{250} \times 100 = 24\%$. The mass is lost because the decomposer microorganisms digest the apple and respire the products, releasing carbon dioxide and water vapour to the air, and because water evaporates from the decaying tissue. The warm room speeds this up, since the microorganisms' enzymes work faster at higher temperatures.

markScheme.description: finds the mass lost, 250 − 190 = 60 g, and divides by the original 250 g (× 100)

questions.prompt: Two identical 300 g samples of grass cuttings are put into compost bins. Sample A, in a warm, well-aerated bin, loses 72 g in 6 days. Sample B, in a cold bin, loses 30 g in 10 days. A student says that sample A decayed 2.4 times as fast as sample B, because 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4. Calculate how many times greater the rate of decay of sample A was than that of sample B.
questions.skill: comparing rates of decay measured over different times
questions.solution: The two masses were lost over **different times**, so each must be turned into a rate first. Sample A: $\dfrac{72}{6} = 12$ g per day. Sample B: $\dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ g per day. Rate of A divided by rate of B $= \dfrac{12}{3} = 4$, so sample A decayed four times as fast, not 2.4 times. The student's comparison ignored the fact that sample B was given 10 days to lose its 30 g. The warm bin speeds up the decomposers' enzymes, and good aeration supplies the oxygen they need for aerobic respiration, which is why composters keep heaps warm, moist and turned.

markScheme.description: converts both losses to rates: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 g per day and 30 ÷ 10 = 3 g per day
divides the rate for A by the rate for B

questions.prompt: A farmer grows wheat in a field and harvests the whole crop every year. Explain why the soil would gradually run short of nitrates if the farmer did nothing about it, and describe two ways the farmer can restore the nitrates in the soil.
questions.solution: Wheat plants absorb **nitrates** from the soil through their roots and use the nitrogen to make amino acids and **proteins**. In a natural ecosystem the plants die and decomposers break their proteins down, returning the nitrogen to the soil as ammonia, which nitrifying bacteria turn back into nitrates. Harvesting removes the whole crop, so the nitrogen in it **never returns**, and each year the soil holds less nitrate. The farmer can add **fertiliser**: either artificial fertiliser that contains nitrates, or manure and compost, which decomposers break down to release nitrogen compounds. Or the farmer can use **crop rotation**, growing a legume such as clover or beans in some years. Their root nodules hold **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** that convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds, and the roots and nodules left behind, or the whole plant ploughed in, return this nitrogen to the soil.

markScheme.description: the wheat takes up nitrates to make proteins, and harvesting removes the plants so the nitrogen is not returned to the soil by decomposition
one way: artificial fertiliser containing nitrates; manure or compost broken down by decomposers; or crop rotation with a legume whose root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria
a second, different way from the same list

criteria.text: Explains that the wheat takes up nitrates to make proteins, and that harvesting the whole crop removes this nitrogen, so it is not returned to the soil when the plants decay

Describes one way of restoring nitrates: artificial fertiliser containing nitrates; manure or compost, which decomposers break down to release ammonia that becomes nitrates; or crop rotation with a legume whose root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Describes a second, different way from the same list

questions.modelAnswer: Plants need nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins, and they get it by absorbing nitrates from the soil through their roots. In a natural ecosystem the nitrogen goes round in a cycle: when plants die, decomposers break down their proteins and release ammonia into the soil, and nitrifying bacteria convert the ammonia into nitrates that the next plants can use. Harvesting breaks this cycle. The whole wheat crop is taken away, so the nitrogen locked in its proteins leaves the field and never comes back, and every year the soil has less nitrate in it, so the yield falls. The farmer has two main ways of restoring the nitrates. The first is to add fertiliser. Artificial fertilisers contain nitrates that the crop can take up straight away, while manure and compost are broken down by decomposers in the soil, releasing ammonia that the nitrifying bacteria turn into nitrates. The second is crop rotation. Instead of wheat every year, the farmer grows a legume, such as clover, peas or beans, in some years. Legumes have nodules on their roots containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds. The roots and nodules left in the soil, and the whole plant if it is ploughed back in rather than harvested, are broken down so that those nitrogen compounds are released by decomposers and converted into nitrates for the wheat that follows.

questions.prompt: A bottle garden is a large glass bottle containing soil, soil microorganisms and a small plant. It was sealed with a cork decades ago and has never been opened, yet the plant is still alive and growing. Explain how carbon continues to cycle inside the sealed bottle, and explain why the garden would die if the microorganisms in the soil were killed.
questions.skill: the carbon cycle in a closed system
questions.solution: Nothing enters or leaves the bottle, so the same carbon atoms are used over and over. The plant takes carbon dioxide from the air in the bottle by **photosynthesis** and builds it into glucose and then into its own biomass. Carbon dioxide is returned to the air by **respiration**: by the plant itself, day and night, and by the **decomposer microorganisms** in the soil, which digest the leaves and roots the plant sheds and respire the products. Decomposition also releases the **mineral ions**, including nitrates, locked in the dead material, so the plant can use them again. If the microorganisms were killed, dead leaves would pile up undecayed; the carbon and the nitrates in them would be **locked away**, the carbon dioxide in the bottle's air would run down as the plant fixed it, the soil would run out of nitrates, and the plant would stop growing and die.

markScheme.description: the plant removes carbon dioxide from the bottle's air by photosynthesis and builds it into glucose and biomass
respiration by the plant and by the decomposer microorganisms, which digest dead leaves and roots, returns carbon dioxide to the air
without decomposers the carbon in dead material stays locked away and the carbon dioxide in the air runs out, or the nitrates are not returned to the soil, so the plant dies

criteria.text: Explains that the plant takes carbon dioxide from the air in the bottle by photosynthesis and builds the carbon into glucose and its own biomass
Explains that carbon dioxide is returned to the air by respiration, both by the plant and by the decomposer microorganisms that digest the dead leaves and roots the plant sheds

Explains that without decomposers the dead material would not be broken down, so its carbon would stay locked away and the carbon dioxide in the bottle's air would be used up, or its nitrates would not return to the soil, so the plant could not keep growing and would die

questions.modelAnswer: A sealed bottle is a complete ecosystem in miniature. It gains light energy through the glass, but no matter gets in or out, so every carbon atom in it has to be used again and again. The plant removes carbon dioxide from the air inside the bottle by photosynthesis, using light energy to combine it with water to make glucose, which it turns into the cellulose, starch and proteins of its leaves, stem and roots. Carbon dioxide gets back into the air by respiration. The plant respires all the time, releasing some of the carbon it fixed, and when it sheds old leaves and roots the decomposer bacteria and fungi in the soil digest them and respire the products, releasing the rest. Decomposition also returns the mineral ions in the dead material, especially the nitrates the plant needs for proteins, to the soil. In this way the carbon cycles between the air, the plant, the dead material and the decomposers, and the water cycles too, evaporating from the leaves and condensing on the glass. If the microorganisms were killed, the cycle would break. Dead leaves would pile up without decaying, and the carbon and nitrogen in them would be locked away. The plant would keep removing carbon dioxide from the small volume of air until there was too little left for photosynthesis, the soil would run out of nitrates, and the plant would stop growing and die. Decomposers are as essential to the cycle as the producer is.

questions.prompt: Explain how a nitrogen atom in the air can become part of a protein in a cow, and how it can later return to the air. Name the types of bacteria involved at each stage.
questions.solution: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas, because its molecules are too unreactive. **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** in the soil and in the root nodules of legumes convert nitrogen gas into **ammonia** and other nitrogen compounds. **Nitrifying bacteria** convert ammonia into **nitrates**. Plants absorb nitrates through their roots by active transport and use them to make **amino acids**, which they join into **proteins**. A cow eats the grass, digests its proteins into amino acids and builds them into its own proteins, so the nitrogen atom is now part of the cow. The cow passes nitrogen out in **urea** in its urine and in faeces, and when it dies its body is broken down by **decomposers**, which release the nitrogen as ammonia; nitrifying bacteria turn this back into nitrates for plants to use again. Nitrogen returns to the air when **denitrifying bacteria**, which thrive in waterlogged soil with little oxygen, convert nitrates back into **nitrogen gas**.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that plants take up nitrates and animals get nitrogen by eating plants, or names one type of bacteria with its role, with little linking into a cycle

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): follows most of the route, nitrogen fixation, nitrates taken up to make proteins, the cow eating the plant, and decomposition or denitrification, naming at least two types of bacteria correctly, but with a gap, such as missing nitrifying bacteria or the return to the air

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a complete cycle: nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas to ammonia or nitrogen compounds; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates; plants absorb nitrates and make amino acids and proteins; the cow digests plant protein and builds its own; decomposers break down urea, faeces and dead bodies to ammonia, which is nitrified again; and denitrifying bacteria return nitrates to the air as nitrogen gas

criteria.text: Explains that plants cannot use nitrogen gas, and that nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil or in the root nodules of legumes convert it into ammonia or other nitrogen compounds
States that nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrates in the soil
Explains that plants absorb nitrates through their roots and use them to make amino acids, which are joined into proteins
Explains that the cow eats the plant, digests its proteins into amino acids and uses them to build its own proteins
Explains that decomposers break down the cow's urea and faeces, and its body when it dies, releasing ammonia, which nitrifying bacteria convert back into nitrates
Explains that denitrifying bacteria, especially in waterlogged soil with little oxygen, convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air

questions.modelAnswer:
**Into the soil.** About four fifths of the air is nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use it, because the two atoms in each molecule are held together so strongly that the molecule is almost unreactive. **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria**, living free in the soil and inside the root nodules of legumes such as clover and beans, can break it: they convert nitrogen gas into **ammonia** and other nitrogen compounds. A little nitrogen is also fixed by lightning. **Nitrifying bacteria** in the soil then convert ammonia into **nitrates**.

**Into the plant.** Nitrates dissolve in soil water and are absorbed by the root hair cells, by active transport where the soil is dilute. The plant combines the nitrogen with the sugars from photosynthesis to make **amino acids**, and joins the amino acids into **proteins** such as enzymes and the proteins of its cell membranes.

**Into the cow.** The cow eats the grass. Its digestive enzymes break the plant proteins down into amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood and used to build the cow's own proteins: muscle, enzymes and milk protein. The nitrogen atom that started in the air is now part of the cow.

**Back to the soil.** The cow excretes surplus nitrogen as **urea** in its urine, and passes undigested protein out in faeces. When the cow, or the grass, dies, its body is broken down by **decomposers**, bacteria and fungi, which release the nitrogen as ammonia. The nitrifying bacteria convert this ammonia into nitrates once more, and the nitrates are taken up by the next generation of plants. This is the loop that keeps a meadow fertile without any fertiliser.

**Back to the air.** **Denitrifying bacteria** do the reverse of fixation: they convert nitrates back into **nitrogen gas**, which escapes to the atmosphere. They thrive in waterlogged soil, where there is little oxygen, which is why a flooded field is left short of nitrates. Farmers counter these losses by adding fertiliser, by rotating crops with legumes, and by draining their soil so the denitrifiers have less to work with.

examTechnique.body:
For any cycle, say which processes take the element out of the abiotic world and which return it. Getting the direction right is most of the marks.

Name the organisms doing each process, not just the process. Plants and algae photosynthesise; all organisms respire; microorganisms decompose.

When asked about the role of microorganisms, say what would happen without them: the elements would stay locked in dead material.

For the nitrogen cycle, name the type of bacteria as well as what it does. Nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying and denitrifying are three different things.

For a rate of decay calculation, find the change first, then divide by the time, then check whether grams or a percentage was asked for.

When explaining decay, refer to the microorganisms and their enzymes rather than to the food itself.
examinerErrors: Saying respiration removes carbon dioxide from the air.
Forgetting that plants respire as well as photosynthesise.
Saying plants absorb nitrogen gas from the air.
Saying a fridge kills the microorganisms rather than slowing their enzymes.
Giving the rate of decay without a unit.
Describing fertiliser pollution as the nitrates poisoning the fish directly.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer sees the three cycles as one shape — something takes the element into living things, something returns it — and can therefore reconstruct a cycle it has half forgotten. It names decomposers in the carbon and nitrogen cycles and says what would happen without them. On fertiliser pollution it gives the full chain from algae through light to decomposers to oxygen, rather than asserting that nitrates are poisonous. It explains decay in terms of the microorganisms' enzymes, which is what makes the denaturing limit obvious rather than arbitrary. And it checks which unit a rate question wants before calculating.
